caption: A developer used Claude Code to create a file-sharing system that can transfer data between two phones using only a screen and a camera, without relying on Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or any physical connection.  The system works by turning a file into a sequence of animated QR codes displayed on one phone’s screen, while the second phone scans and reconstructs the data through its camera. It uses fountain codes, where each frame contains a combination of random file segments, allowing the transfer to continue even if some frames are missed.  The project can transfer a 2 MB image at around 129 KB/s. Built in a single night, the tool has also been released as open source.  The idea actually started from a music-related challenge. The developer wanted to avoid streaming limitations and ads while creating a cached web-based MP3 player. While using Claude Code, they needed a way to move tracks between phones without requiring both devices to be connected to the same network.  The solution? Using rapidly changing QR codes as a wireless bridge between devices. creator: _researchrover
caption: Not all literature reviews serve the same purpose and choosing the wrong one can weaken your entire research.  One of the most common mistakes I see among students and early-career researchers is treating every literature review as if it’s the same.  The truth is, your research objective should determine the type of literature review you choose.  📖 Here’s a simple way to think about it:  🔹 Narrative Review – Best for providing a broad understanding of a topic.  🔹 Systematic Literature Review (SLR) – Ideal when you need a structured, transparent, and reproducible synthesis of evidence.  🔹 Scoping Review – Perfect for exploring emerging fields, identifying research gaps, and mapping existing evidence.  🔹 Integrative Review – Combines findings from different research methodologies to provide a comprehensive perspective.  🔹 Theoretical Review – Focuses on theories, models, and conceptual frameworks rather than empirical findings.  🔹 Critical Review – Goes beyond summarizing literature by evaluating strengths, limitations, and inconsistencies.  🔹 Meta-analysis – Statistically combines results from multiple quantitative studies to produce stronger evidence.  🔹 Meta-synthesis – Integrates findings from qualitative studies to generate deeper insights.  🔹 Rapid Review – A faster approach designed for policy-making and time-sensitive decisions.  🔹 Umbrella Review – Synthesizes evidence from multiple systematic reviews, offering the highest level of evidence in many fields.  📌 Remember: The best literature review isn’t the most complex one  it’s the one that aligns with your research question, objectives, and methodology. caption: Inferno By Herri met de Bles (16th century) Palazzo Ducale (Doge’s Palace), Venice  Not a painting of Hell. A painting that feels like you have already entered it. An enormous dark sphere fills the sky, blotting out anything above — there is no heaven to look up to here, only a ceiling. Along the horizon every city burns. In the centre, naked figures crowd around a red structure and wait, while others are already inside, packed behind a spiked gate. They are not being tortured. They are being processed. On the left, a monk and a nun haul a cart under a demon’s whip: Bles putting the clergy in Hell and making them carry the weight of everyone they failed. And in a bed, a man and a woman lie under the covers with a demon leaning over them and a frog squatting on the blanket — in the sixteenth century, the frog meant lust. Their private sin, made permanent and public.  #arthistory #symbolisminart #paintingexplained #oldmasters

caption: Context: "My dogmatic slumber was interrupted..." — Immanuel Kant  For years, Immanuel Kant pursued his philosophical inquiries within the comfortable framework of traditional rationalism, convinced that human reason alone could unlock the ultimate truths of metaphysics. He moved through the academic world of Königsberg with methodical precision, holding a firm belief in necessary truths and the innate architecture of the mind. However, this intellectual tranquility was abruptly shattered when he came across the skeptical writings of the Scottish philosopher David Hume. Hume’s rigorous critique, particularly his bold assertion that cause and effect relationships are merely habits of observation rather than objectively demonstrable truths, struck at the very foundation of Kant's worldview.  Reading Hume's essays between 1769 and 1772 acted as a sudden intellectual jolt, pulling Kant out of his long standing conceptual comfort zone. Rather than falling into total skepticism, Kant channeled this shock into a revolutionary paradigm shift. Realizing that reason could no longer be taken for granted without questioning its own limits, he set out to dismantle and rebuild the foundations of epistemology itself. This intense period of reorientation paved the way for his monumental Critique of Pure Reason, forever altering the landscape of modern philosophy.

caption: Wolff's Division of the Sciences: A Historical Philosophical Framework This academic diagram, titled "Wolff's Division of the Sciences," illustrates the systematic classification of human knowledge proposed by the influential German Enlightenment philosopher Christian Wolff. Rooted in the 18th-century rationalist tradition, this hierarchical tree breaks down all intellectual disciplines into a structured, logical order originating from Knowledge. Core Branches of Knowledge At the highest level, knowledge is divided into three primary categories: History (fact), Philosophy (reason of the fact), and Mathematics (quantity of things). The bulk of the diagram focuses on Philosophy, which Wolff subdivides into two major domains: "of things" (theoretical philosophy) and "of human actions" (practical philosophy). 1. Philosophy of Things (Theoretical Knowledge) This branch is further split into two key areas:  * Metaphysics (Pneumatics): Encompasses Ontology (being in general), Natural Theology (God), Psychology (human souls), and General Cosmology (world in general). Together, these study abstract and spiritual realities.  * Physics (Bodies): Covers empirical and natural sciences, branching into General physics (affections of bodies), Cosmology (world as such), Meteorology (atmospheric phenomena), Oryctology (minerals), Hydrology (water), Phytology (plants), Physiology (animated bodies), and Teleology (final causes of natural things). 2. Philosophy of Human Actions (Practical Knowledge) This domain deals with human agency, logic, and societal organization, categorized under three headings:  * Cognitive: Focuses on mental processes, including Logic (direction of mind to truth) and Ars inveniendi (discovery of latent truth).  * Appetitive: Pertains to morality and societal structures, featuring Jus naturae (knowledge of good and evil), Universal practical philosophy, Ethics (individual morality), Politics (civil society), and Oeconomica (lesser societies/households).  * Productive and Technology: Covers practical arts and communication, including Grammatical, Rhetorical, and Poetical philosophy, alongside Technology (agriculture, civil architecture, etc.).
